idiom_name: module-level shared instance (duck typing) / SimpleNamespace; contextlib.nullcontext, logging.NullHandler
implementation_notes: Python does not need a hierarchy: any object whose attributes are callables with benign bodies satisfies the interface, so the special case is usually a single module-level instance of a small class - or even types.SimpleNamespace(info=lambda *a, **k: None) when the interface is trivial. The standard library ships the same object for optional infrastructure: contextlib.nullcontext is a context manager that does nothing, and logging.NullHandler is a handler that discards records, both explicitly described as no-op stand-ins. Prefer a real object over None when call sites should stay branch-free; return None (or a dataclass with an explicit absent flag) when the caller must be forced to handle the case.
code_sketch:
class _UnknownCustomer:
    name = "occupant"
    balance = Decimal("0")
    bills: tuple = ()
    def is_unknown(self) -> bool: return True

UNKNOWN_CUSTOMER = _UnknownCustomer()      # one shared, stateless instance
def find_customer(cid): return _repo.get(cid) or UNKNOWN_CUSTOMER
pitfalls: Truthiness: a valid object that defines __bool__ as False (an empty collection, a zero value) is silently replaced by the special case in `x or default`; test `is None` in the factory.
Module-level instances are shared by every importer, so mutating an attribute changes the special case process-wide; keep it immutable or make it a frozen dataclass.
Nothing checks a duck-typed special case against the interface: a renamed or added method fails only at the call site, so keep the two implementations side by side and run shared tests.
contextlib.nullcontext and None are not interchangeable: nullcontext exists precisely so that `with cm:` stays uniform, and passing None where a context manager is expected still fails.
